cues.text: Striking at the Church's Leadership
In 257, the Emperor Valerian , whose earlier years in power had shown surprising tolerance toward Christians, reversed course sharply.

He issued a first edict banishing bishops and priests from their sees and forbidding Christian assemblies, particularly in the cemeteries where the faithful gathered to honor their martyrs and celebrate the Eucharist.
Valerian's earlier reign had in fact seen Christians serving openly at court and in the imperial household.
This made his sudden reversal all the more disorienting to a Church that had, by the mid-250s, grown accustomed to a real if fragile toleration.
A Second, Harsher Edict
When this initial measure failed to break the Church's resolve, Valerian issued a far more severe decree the following year.
It ordered the immediate execution of bishops, priests, and deacons.
Christian senators and knights who refused to recant lost their rank and property.
Christian women of standing and members of the imperial household faced exile or forced labor.
This was a deliberate strategy aimed squarely at the Church's leadership and its wealthier, more socially prominent members.
A Pope Killed at the Altar
Among the persecution's earliest and most memorable casualties was Pope Sixtus II .
According to treasured tradition, he was seized and beheaded while presiding at the liturgy within the catacombs outside Rome.
Several of his own deacons, arrested alongside him in the same underground assembly, also suffered death.
Lawrence and the Treasures of the Church
Spared for a few additional days, the Roman deacon Lawrence was ordered by the city prefect to surrender the Church's treasures.
He famously presented instead a gathering of Rome's poor, sick, and disabled, declaring these — not gold or silver — to be the Church's true wealth.
Enraged by what he took for open defiance, the prefect condemned Lawrence to a slow death by fire, a martyrdom that made an unusually deep and lasting impression on the whole city of Rome.
Cyprian's Steady Witness
In North Africa, Bishop Cyprian of Carthage — already the Church's most experienced pastoral guide through the earlier crisis of the lapsi under Decius — was exiled under the first edict.

When the second and harsher decree arrived, he was arrested, tried, and beheaded before a public gathering, meeting his sentence with the same calm, unhurried dignity that had marked the whole of his episcopate, his own deacon recorded.

Rome's own popular memory of Lawrence's calm defiance before his execution would outlive the empire itself, inspiring devotion, art, and even architecture for the whole of the two millennia that followed.
A Persecution That Judged Its Own Author
The persecution ended abruptly in 260, when Valerian himself was captured by the Persian king Shapur I during a disastrous military campaign.
He was the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by a foreign power and, according to later Christian tradition, endured prolonged humiliation in captivity until his death.
Ancient Christian writers read this fate as a fitting and almost providential judgment on the emperor who had tried to silence the Church's shepherds.

Valerian's son and successor, Gallienus, restored peace to the Church almost immediately upon taking power, formally returning confiscated property and inaugurating nearly four decades of relative calm before the far greater trial of Diocletian's persecution still lay ahead.
The three martyrdoms remembered most vividly from this persecution were a pope killed at the altar, a deacon roasted for his wit and charity, and a bishop beheaded with unshaken composure.
Together, they gave the Roman Church some of its most enduring and frequently retold stories of courage, still recounted, prayed over, and depicted in art some seventeen centuries later.

Even Valerian's own captor, according to later Christian writers, could not undo what his edicts had failed to accomplish: the Church he tried to decapitate simply grew a new generation of shepherds within the very decade of his death.
